The single habit that changed how I build: cutting scope until shipping feels almost too easy.

The projects I've finished all have one thing in common: they were
embarrassingly small when they launched.

The ones I abandoned? All ambitious.

## Scope is the enemy

A feature you can ship this week beats a system you can ship this quarter.
Every extra week of building is a week of zero feedback — and feedback is
the only thing that tells you whether you're building the right thing at all.

> If you're not slightly embarrassed by v1, you shipped too late.

## My rule of thumb

Before starting anything, I ask: **what's the version of this I could ship
in two days?** Then I build *that*. Not as a prototype — as the actual
release.

Most of the time, the two-day version turns out to be all anyone needed.

Pomodoro Sudah Ga Relevan Lagi. Kenalan Sama Flowmodoro.
Pomodoro ngukur berapa lama kamu harus kerja, flowmodoro ngukur berapa lama kamu bisa fokus — dan kenapa itu jauh lebih relevan buat ritme kerja sekarang.

Coba jujur sama diri sendiri: kapan terakhir kali kamu kerja 25 menit, terus timer bunyi, dan kamu langsung berhenti — padahal lagi asik-asiknya?

Kalau pernah, berarti kamu udah ngerasain sendiri masalah terbesar dari Pomodoro Technique: dia dibangun buat lawan distraksi, bukan buat manfaatin focus.

## Pomodoro Lahir di Dunia yang Beda

Francesco Cirillo bikin Pomodoro tahun 1980-an, pake timer dapur berbentuk tomat. Konteksnya waktu itu: dunia kerja yang linear, minim notifikasi, minim tab browser yang berkedip-kedip minta perhatian. 25 menit kerja, 5 menit istirahat — angka ini masuk akal karena musuh utamanya cuma satu: rasa males mulai.

Masalahnya, dunia kita sekarang beda total. Musuh kita bukan cuma males mulai. Musuh kita adalah:

- Notifikasi yang dateng tiap 3-4 menit
- Context switching antar tools yang bikin otak capek duluan sebelum kerja beneran mulai
- Ritme kerja yang ga lagi seragam — kadang butuh 10 menit buat deep dive, kadang butuh 90 menit dan ga mau diganggu

Di dunia kayak gini, timer 25 menit yang fix itu justru jadi masalah baru. Dia motong flow di saat yang salah.

## Konsep yang Hilang: Focus Retention Time

Ini yang menurutku jadi akar masalahnya — dan jarang dibahas orang.

**Focus retention time** adalah durasi realistis kamu bisa nahan atensi penuh sebelum otak mulai nyari alasan buat kabur. Ini bukan angka tetap. Dia berubah-ubah tergantung:

- Jenis tugasnya (nulis vs riset vs eksekusi teknis)
- Jam berapa kamu ngerjain (pagi vs setelah makan siang)
- Seberapa capek kognitif kamu hari itu
- Seberapa "masuk" kamu ke tugas itu — udah warm-up atau belum

Pomodoro nganggep focus retention time itu konstan: 25 menit, titik. Padahal kenyataannya fluktuatif. Kadang kamu baru "masuk" di menit ke-20, terus di-interupsi timer pas lagi di puncak fokus. Kadang kamu udah capek di menit ke-12 tapi timer maksa lanjut sampe 25.

Di sinilah sistem yang rigid ketemu masalahnya sendiri: dia optimasi buat kepatuhan pada jadwal, bukan buat ngikutin kondisi fokus yang sebenarnya.

## Kenalan Sama Flowmodoro

Flowmodoro membalik logikanya. Alih-alih nentuin durasi kerja di depan, kamu **kerja sampai fokusnya beneran habis**, baru istirahat — dan durasi istirahatnya proporsional sama seberapa dalam kamu tadi fokus.

Cara kerjanya simpel:

1. **Mulai kerja tanpa timer kerja.** Kamu cuma nyalain stopwatch buat nyatet berapa lama kamu beneran fokus.
2. **Berhenti kerja begitu fokus mulai pecah** — bukan karena alarm bunyi, tapi karena kamu ngerasa sendiri atensinya udah bocor (mulai mikirin hal lain, mulai pengen buka tab baru, dst).
3. **Istirahat proporsional.** Aturan umumnya sekitar 1 banding 5: kalau kamu fokus 40 menit, istirahat 8 menit. Fokus 15 menit, istirahat 3 menit.
4. **Ulangi**, dan dari situ kamu mulai punya data nyata soal focus retention time kamu sendiri — bukan angka generik yang dipaksain dari luar.

Bedanya sama Pomodoro kentara: Pomodoro tanya "berapa lama harus kerja?" Flowmodoro tanya "berapa lama aku BISA fokus, hari ini, buat tugas ini?"

## Kenapa Ini Cocok Buat Sistem yang Lebih Personal

Ini yang bikin aku tertarik ngangkat topik ini di awal. Flowmodoro bukan sekadar "teknik produktivitas baru" — dia ngajarin kamu buat mulai ngenal pola fokus kamu sendiri dari waktu ke waktu. Itu data personal yang jauh lebih berharga daripada sekadar ngikutin sistem orang lain.

Dan ini nyambung ke hal yang lebih besar: kalau kita mau bikin sistem produktivitas yang beneran nempel — bukan yang dipaksain — titik mulainya bukan dari mencari teknik yang "katanya work buat semua orang". Titik mulainya dari ngerti ritme fokus diri sendiri dulu.

Di tulisan berikutnya, aku bakal bahas gimana cara nge-track focus retention time ini secara praktis, dan gimana pola ini bisa disambungin ke checkpoint-checkpoint harian — termasuk momen-momen kayak waktu sholat yang secara alami udah jadi jeda dalam ritme hari kita.

Mau langsung nyobain? Ada **[Pomodoro & Flowmodoro Timer](/resources/pomodoro-timer/)** — timer fokus minimalis yang bisa kamu pakai buat mode flowmodoro hari ini juga.

A minimal, distraction-free focus timer. Classic 25/5 pomodoro or flowmodoro — focus as long as you flow, break for a fifth of it.

## About this tool

Two timers in one, and nothing else on the screen:

- **Pomodoro** — the classic: 25 minutes of focus, 5 minutes of break, on repeat.
- **Flowmodoro** — no fixed blocks. Focus as long as you're in flow; when you take a break, you earn one fifth of your focus time.

It also keeps simple statistics for the day — total focus time, sessions,
average focus length, and your focus : break ratio — stored only in your
browser.

- Runs entirely in your browser — nothing is sent anywhere
- Works offline once loaded
- Keyboard friendly: <kbd>Space</kbd> to start / take a break, <kbd>S</kbd> to stop

If it helps you, share it with a friend.

Where science meets sunnah — a daily rhythm planner combining ultradian focus cycles, circadian energy, and sunnah time management. Your day starts at Maghrib.

## About this tool

A daily rhythm planner built on a simple idea: the productivity science of
ultradian cycles and circadian energy fits naturally with how the sunnah
already structures a day.

- **Day starts at Maghrib** — the Islamic day begins at sunset, and so does your timeline (with both Gregorian and Hijri dates).
- **Ultradian cycles** — free time between anchors is filled with 90-minute deep-focus blocks and 20-minute breaks.
- **Circadian awareness** — each block is labeled with your likely energy level (peak, trough, rebound) so you match the task to the hour.
- **Sunnah anchors** — the five prayers, dhuha, qailulah before Dhuhr, and qiyamullail frame the schedule; a guide panel explains each.
- **Prayer times by location** — one tap fetches accurate times for where you are (with manual override).
- Write a target for every focus block, close the day with a reflection, and export it all to your clipboard.

Settings, notes, and reflections are saved in your browser — nothing is sent anywhere. Available in Bahasa Indonesia and English.

Plant habits as a cue → routine → reward loop. Miss a day and you get a shrunk-down fallback to save the streak; only honest failure earns a burial in the cemetery.

A habit garden that's honest about failure.

- **Plan the loop** — build each habit as *after what → I will → payoff*, with the sentence writing itself as you type.
- **Streaks that grow** — your plant sprouts leaves and blooms as the streak climbs, and flatlines when you miss two days.

- **The cemetery** — when a habit really dies, bury it with an honest cause and a note, and learn which killers keep coming back.
- **Resurrect** — dig one up and plant it again from scratch.

The 9×9 goal grid Noboru Harada taught and Shohei Ohtani famously used — one core ambition, eight pillars, 64 micro-actions. Edit a pillar and every sub-grid stays in sync; check tasks and watch the percentages climb.

## About this tool

The 9×9 goal grid from the Harada Method — the technique Noboru Harada developed and Shohei Ohtani used to map out his baseball dream. A 3×3 master grid sits around one core ambition, and each surrounding cell expands into its own 3×3 sub-grid of micro-actions.

- **Core ambition** — your single most important goal sits in the dead center of the master grid.
- **Eight pillars** — the surrounding cells; type a pillar here and it auto-fills the center of its sub-grid everywhere.
- **64 micro-actions** — eight small, tactical tasks per pillar, each with its own completion toggle.
- **Macro view** — see the whole 9×9 map at a glance, with a color-coded overview per pillar (blue = has content, green = done).
- **Focus view** — zoom into one pillar for a mobile-friendly, color-coded editing board.
- **Live progress** — per-pillar percentage and an overall completion score, updated as you tick tasks.
- **Export / Import** — download your grid as JSON and restore it anywhere.
- **Print / PDF** — a clean, print-ready layout of the full grid.

Saved in your browser only — nothing is sent anywhere.
